title: Lawyers sanctioned for fake AI citations: verify each one on Mac before filing in 2026
metaTitle: Lawyers Sanctioned for Fake AI Citations: Verify Before Filing
description: Courts have sanctioned lawyers for fake AI citations. Here is what it costs, why it happens, and a free routine to check every case before you file.
targetKeyword: lawyers sanctioned for fake AI citations
intro: Lawyers get sanctioned for fake AI citations when a filing cites cases that do not exist, or says real cases say things they do not. Courts have fined lawyers $5,000 and $10,000 for it. The fix is a cite-check you do yourself, on every authority, before anything reaches the court.
tldr: Courts have sanctioned lawyers for fabricated AI citations, with fines of $5,000 and $10,000 in two cases.
Real-looking citations are the trap. Wrong holdings and invented quotes get lawyers in trouble too.
A Stanford study found legal research tools hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time. Vendor claims are not proof.
A manual check of each case, quote and holding costs nothing and needs no special software.
Lazur can point, explain and dictate. It cannot confirm that a case exists.

blocks.text: What lawyers sanctioned for fake AI citations pay

Start with the cost you can see. Courts have fined lawyers for AI fake citations. In Mata v. Avianca, Judge P. Kevin Castel ordered the plaintiff's attorneys to pay $5,000 for AI-fabricated case citations. In Noland v. Land of the Free, a California appeals court sanctioned plaintiff's counsel $10,000 for fabricated citations and quotations.

The fine is rarely the whole bill. Courts now ask who noticed a fake, and when. In Noland, the court declined to award fees to opposing counsel who did not flag the fakes before the order to show cause. In Torres Campos v. Munoz, a trial court adopted a proposed order that cited two fake cases. Opposing counsel had not flagged them. The appeals court declined to excuse the appellant's forfeiture.
Why it costs more time than it looks

The sources I could open do not measure how long a cite-check takes. Thomson Reuters expects legal professionals to free up nearly 240 hours per year with AI, worth an average $19,000 per professional. That is expected time saved. The report does not explain its math or address verification.
For a rough reference, the BLS median lawyer wage was $76.76 per hour in May 2025. That is a salary equivalent, not a billing rate. Use it only to size an hour of your time, not to price your work.

blocks.title: Time your own routine
blocks.text: Pick one authority from your current draft. Time your full check on it, from pulling the case to logging the result. Multiply that by the number of authorities. That number is your real cost, not a vendor's estimate.
How often AI fake citations reach court filings

The count is high. Damien Charlotin's database lists 2,266 cases where AI hallucinations were identified, last updated 5 November 2026. Of those, 1,535 come from the USA. The database counts 898 cases involving lawyers.

Read the number as a floor, not a total. The database is a monitoring list. It includes cases with unconfirmed AI use, and not every entry ended in a sanction. Lawyers are not the only group in it, so compare the groups with care.
Why AI tools invent citations, even legal ones

A general chatbot predicts text. Unless it searches a database, it does not check the case it names. A made-up case can have a plausible name, a court, a reporter number and a year. In the Stanford HAI summary, general chatbots were wrong between 58% and 82% of the time on legal queries.

Legal tools are better, but they are not clean. The Stanford RegLab paper tested Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI. It found each one hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time. The Stanford HAI summary gives different figures, with Westlaw above 34%. The tests reflect 2024 versions of the tools, so current products may differ.

The HAI summary says vendors' 'hallucination-free' claims lacked hard evidence. It concludes that 'legal hallucinations have not been solved.' Read any vendor promise as a claim to test, not a guarantee. Ask for the test data before you rely on it.
A free routine to verify AI citations before filing
This routine costs nothing. It needs your browser, your draft and a simple log. Run it on every authority, including the ones you think you know well.

items: Pull every authority into one table. Cases, statutes, rules and secondary sources all go in.
Open each case from a source you trust, such as your firm's research account or the court's own opinion. A summary is not the case.
Match the case name, court, year and reporter cite to the opinion header.
Search each quoted phrase with ⌘F. If the exact words are not in the opinion, flag the quote.
Read the paragraph your brief relies on. Confirm it supports your exact point, not a nearby one.
Check the pin cite. The page or paragraph should contain the language your brief attributes to it.
Log the date, your initials and the source for each check. Keep the log with the file.

blocks.text: Quote checks matter because Noland involved fabricated quotations too. A real case can also be quoted wrong. Search the exact words, not your memory of them. If your draft lives in Word, see [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word) for the review tools you will use.
Check the holding, not just the case name

Here is the trap that catches experienced lawyers. A brief cites a real case for a rule it never states. The name is right, the court is right, and the year is right. Only the paragraph shows that the rule is not there.

rows: Opens from a trusted source with the same name and court
A similar name that belongs to a different case
Matches the header of the opinion
A lower court opinion cited as if it came from a higher court
Exact words appear with the same punctuation
A paraphrase presented inside quotation marks
The paragraph supports your exact point
A dissent or a passing remark used as the rule
The page or paragraph contains the language
A pin that points to an unrelated page
blocks.caption: A five-step check for each authority in a brief

blocks.text: Say your draft states that a court held a notice rule applies to your facts. The case is real. Open the opinion and find the passage. The rule appears in a dissent, and the majority did not adopt it. A weak holding became a strong sentence, and the fix is to change the sentence or cite the majority.
Check the other side's citations too

Courts now expect you to check the other side. In Nuvola v. Wright in Hennepin County, the court said citations to fictional cases should not be left for the court to catch alone. It said counsel must include 'completing a basic cite-check of the cases cited by the other side.'

Thomas Wilkinson, quoted in the ABA Journal, called failing to catch opponents' fakes 'a matter of perceived competence.' Whether or not you agree, the risk to your reputation is the same. Run the same routine on the other side's brief, and log it.
Mac tools and paid checkers, honestly

Paid checkers can save time, but they do not replace your read. Westlaw Edge Quick Check, from Thomson Reuters, checks citations with KeyCite. It gives warnings for cited authority, an analysis of quotations and a table of authorities. It can also analyze an opponent's brief. Check Thomson Reuters' pricing page for current cost.

Clearbrief runs as a task pane inside Microsoft Word, from the Microsoft AppSource store. Its page lists Solo pricing at $300 per user per month. It says its checks 'can't hallucinate,' which is a vendor claim with no independent test on the page. The page does not say whether it works in Word for Mac.

CiteMatch is in private testing, by invitation only. It is free for legal aid, clinics and pro bono programs. Its site says 'Please do not send client files.' Its macOS support is not confirmed. I could not find a native Mac citation checker.

Before you pay for anything, ask the vendor three things in writing. Does it run on macOS? Which Word version does it need? Where do my files go? I found no controlled study showing that any of these workflows lowers filed-citation errors.
What Lazur can and cannot do for citation checks

Lazur sees your screen while you hold the shortcut. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where something is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask what a warning means, and Lazur answers out loud. This helps when a checker's menu hides the next step.

Lazur does not click buttons or operate apps for you. In guide mode it walks you through one click at a time, and it waits for each one. It is not a citator. It cannot confirm that a case is real or that a quote is accurate.

The research capability runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report. Use it to collect where to look, such as a search result for each case name. Then open the opinion yourself. A summary is a lead, not a check.

Dictation helps with the log. Hold fn and speak, and the text lands at the cursor in any app. Dictation types what you say. It does not check what you say, so proof each line before it goes in the file.

blocks.title: Check firm rules first
blocks.text: Before you show Lazur a client brief, read your firm's AI policy and your jurisdiction's rules on client data. Lazur sends the audio and screenshot to AI providers to answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.
Mistakes that get lawyers in trouble

items: Treating a real case name as proof that the quote and holding are right.
Trusting a citator warning without reading the case it points to.
Assuming a legal research tool cannot hallucinate. The studies say it can.
Pasting AI text into a draft without a note of where it came from.
Leaving the other side's citations unchecked because they filed first.
Running the check the night before the deadline, then skipping the parts you cannot finish.

blocks.text: If a fake citation already reached the court

Do not wait for the judge to find it. Tell your supervising lawyer right away. Then follow your firm's procedure and the court's rules on corrections. Write down the bad citation, where it came from, and what you checked afterward.

The sources I reviewed do not describe correction procedures for any particular court. Read your local rules and your firm's policy before you file a correction. Get a second reader on the wording before it goes out.

faq.question: Can a lawyer be sanctioned for a fake citation the opponent filed?
faq.answer: Courts have faulted lawyers who did not flag fake citations in an opponent's filing. In Nuvola v. Wright, the court said counsel must include a basic cite-check of the cases the other side cites. Use the same routine on their brief that you use on your own.

faq.question: Does a real case name mean the citation is correct?
faq.answer: No. A real case can be cited for a holding it does not state, or quoted with words that are not in the opinion. Check the court, the year, the exact quote and the paragraph your brief relies on.

faq.question: Can Lazur check whether a case exists?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a citator, and it does not confirm that a case is real. It can point at where to look, explain what is on your screen, and draft notes. You still open the opinion yourself.

faq.question: Is the 17% to 33% error rate the same for every tool?
faq.answer: No. The Stanford RegLab paper tested three legal research tools and found rates between 17% and 33%. The Stanford HAI summary gives different figures, with Westlaw above 34%. Both reflect 2024 versions, so test the current product yourself.

faq.question: Is a free routine enough, or do I need a paid checker?
faq.answer: A free manual routine works on any brief and costs nothing. Paid checkers can add speed and quotation analysis. Treat their marketing claims as claims until you test them on your own drafts.

faq.question: Can I show Lazur a client brief?
faq.answer: Follow your firm's AI policy and your jurisdiction's rules on client data first. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Does Clearbrief work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Its page does not say whether it supports Word for Mac or only Windows. Ask the vendor before you pay. The page lists Solo pricing at $300 per user per month.

faq.question: What if I already filed a fake citation?
faq.answer: Tell your supervising lawyer right away. Follow your firm's procedure and the court's correction rules. Keep a written record of what was wrong and what you checked afterward.

faq.question: How long does the routine take?
faq.answer: The sources I could open do not measure it. Time one check on an authority from your own draft, then multiply by the number of authorities in the brief.

costs.title: Fines and sanctions
costs.text: Courts have fined lawyers $5,000 in Mata v. Avianca and $10,000 in Noland v. Land of the Free for fabricated citations. The fine is the cost everyone sees first, and it is rarely the only one.

costs.title: Fees that go to the other side
costs.text: In Noland, the court declined to award fees to opposing counsel who did not flag the fake citations before the order to show cause. Courts now look at who noticed a fake, and when.

costs.title: Forfeited arguments
costs.text: In Torres Campos v. Munoz, a trial court adopted a proposed order that cited two fake cases, and opposing counsel did not flag them. The appeals court declined to excuse the appellant's forfeiture.

costs.title: Trust with the judge
costs.text: A critic quoted by the ABA Journal called failing to catch opponents' fake citations 'a matter of perceived competence.' Judges remember which filings were careful and which were not.

costs.title: Your hours
costs.text: No source I opened measures verification time. Thomson Reuters expects about 240 hours per year of AI time savings, but that is expected savings, not cleanup time. Measure your own routine.

causes.title: Chatbots predict text, they do not look cases up
causes.text: General chatbots write plausible legal text. Unless they search a database, they do not check each case before they write it. In the Stanford HAI summary, general chatbots were wrong between 58% and 82% of the time on legal queries. A fake case can look exactly like a real one.

causes.title: Legal tools still get it wrong
causes.text: Legal-specific tools reduce the risk, but the studies did not find zero. The Stanford RegLab paper found hallucination rates between 17% and 33% for three leading tools. The HAI summary says vendors' hallucination-free claims lacked hard evidence.

causes.title: A real case with wrong words
causes.text: A case can exist and still be cited for a holding it does not contain. It can also be quoted with words that are not in the opinion. Noland involved fabricated quotations as well as fabricated citations. Many errors look right on a quick skim.

causes.title: Copy and paste from a chat window
causes.text: AI text often moves from a chat window into a Word draft. Once it sits in the brief, nobody remembers which sentences came from the tool. A simple log of sources prevents that drift.

causes.title: Trusting the other side to catch it
causes.text: Lawyers often assume the other side will catch fake cases. Courts have pushed back on that habit. In Nuvola v. Wright, the court said the opposing party should not be the last line of defense.

causes.title: Deadlines and promised time savings
causes.text: Thomson Reuters' 2025 report says legal professionals expect AI to free up nearly 240 hours a year. Deadlines make that promise tempting to spend early. The report does not address verification or oversight of AI output.

fixes.title: Keep a verification log
fixes.text: Record the date, your initials, the source and the result for each authority. A log turns I checked it into a record you can show a supervising lawyer. It costs nothing more than a Word table or a page in your notes app.

fixes.title: Search every quoted phrase
fixes.text: Use ⌘F in your browser or PDF viewer to search each quoted phrase in the opinion. Match punctuation and capitalization. A paraphrase inside quotation marks is a red flag, so fix it or drop the quotes.

fixes.title: Read the paragraph, not the summary
fixes.text: Headnotes and case summaries are someone else's words. Read the paragraph your brief depends on, in the opinion itself. Confirm the court actually said the rule your draft states, and no more.

fixes.title: Check the court's own copy
fixes.text: When the court publishes its opinion, use that text to confirm the quotes. If your research account and the court copy differ, trust the court copy and note the difference in your log.

fixes.title: Treat AI output as a list of leads
fixes.text: Ask a tool for cases on a point, then verify each one from scratch. Never file a citation you have not opened. A name in a chat window is a starting point, nothing more.

fixes.title: Get a second reader for heavy citations
fixes.text: Pick the authorities your argument depends on most. Ask a colleague to open each one and read the key paragraph aloud. Two readers catch more than one, and the log shows who checked what.

fixes.title: Run the same routine on opposing briefs
fixes.text: Check every authority in the other side's filing with the same steps. Log what you cannot open or find, and raise the problem with the court promptly under your local rules.

fixes.title: Price paid checkers before you need one
fixes.text: Clearbrief lists Solo pricing at $300 per user per month on its page. Ask whether a checker runs on macOS and where your files go. CiteMatch is free for legal aid, clinics and pro bono programs, by invitation.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Pull the full list
plan.text: Copy every authority from the draft into one Word table. Add columns for source, date and result. Do not start checking until the list is complete, so nothing hides in a footnote.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Open and match
plan.text: Open each case from a trusted source. Match the name, court and year to the opinion header. Mark any mismatch, and do not move on until you know why it happened.

plan.label: Day 1 PM
plan.title: Quotes and pin cites
plan.text: Search each quoted phrase with ⌘F. Confirm each pin cite points to the language your brief attributes to it. Log the result for each one.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Read the holdings
plan.text: Read the paragraph your brief relies on for each case. Confirm the court said the rule you cite. Rewrite any sentence that states a holding more strongly than the opinion does.

plan.label: Day 2 PM
plan.title: Check the other side
plan.text: Run the same steps on the opposing brief. Note each citation you cannot open or find. Decide with your supervising lawyer how and when to raise it.

plan.label: Before filing
plan.title: Second reader
plan.text: Have a colleague open the authorities your argument depends on most. Ask them to read the key paragraph aloud, then initial the log for each one.
